notes.meaning: The Philistines kept the ark for seven months, hoping to hold on to their battle trophy. Yet moving it from city to city brought nothing but painful disease and ruined crops. It took all this time for them to admit they could not defeat the God of Israel.

The Philistine leaders realized they could no longer keep the ark, so they called for their pagan priests and fortune-tellers. They knew they had offended a powerful deity and were afraid of making things worse. They wanted clear instructions on how to return the holy chest safely.

Their religious advisors warned them not to send the ark away empty-handed. They told the leaders to include a guilt offering—a payment meant to make amends for their offense. If their sickness ceased after this, they would know for certain that the Lord had caused their suffering.

The advisors instructed them to craft five gold models of their tumors and five gold rats, one for each Philistine ruler. Because the same plagues had struck both the leaders and the common people, everyone shared the blame and needed relief.

Making models of the things causing their pain was an ancient way of admitting guilt and asking a god for mercy. By sending these gold gifts, the Philistines honored the God of Israel. They hoped He would lift His heavy hand from their bodies, their land, and their own gods.

The priests reminded their people how Pharaoh and the Egyptians had stubbornly refused to listen to the Lord until disaster crushed them. They warned that resisting Israel's God was foolish and would only bring deeper ruin. It was better to let the ark go freely than to be broken by more plagues.

The priests set up an impossible test to prove whether God was truly behind their troubles. They hitched two nursing cows that had never worn a yoke to a brand-new cart, then locked their calves away in a barn. Naturally, mother cows would resist a yoke and fight to return home to feed their babies.

The Philistines were told to place the ark on the wagon and put the golden guilt offerings into a small chest next to it. Using an unused cart was an attempt to show respect to a holy object. Then they let the cart roll away on its own, with no human driver to lead the cows.

The leaders watched closely to see which direction the animals would choose. If the cows walked straight toward the Israelite town of Beth-shemesh, it would prove God had sent the disasters. If the cows turned back to their calves, the Philistines would conclude that their sickness had happened purely by accident.
The men followed the instructions down to the last detail. They harnessed two milk cows to the new cart and shut their calves away in the barn to see what the cows would do.

They loaded the ark onto the wagon along with the box containing the golden rats and tumor models. The Philistines were now eager to send off their valuable prize to save themselves from further harm.

Overcoming their natural instincts, the untrained cows walked straight down the road toward Israel without veering to the right or the left. They cried out for their calves the whole way, yet an unseen power guided them forward. The Philistine rulers followed behind in amazement, receiving undeniable proof of God's power.

Israelite farmers were busy reaping their wheat crop in the valley when they suddenly spotted the ark approaching. They had made no effort to rescue it, yet God returned it to them by His own power. The sight of the sacred chest filled the workers with overwhelming joy.

The cart rolled into the field of a man named Joshua and halted right by a giant rock. The reapers chopped up the wooden cart for firewood and sacrificed the two cows as a burnt offering to the Lord, dedicating themselves anew to His service.

differ.view: The sacrifice strictly broke the rules of the law by offering female animals away from the tabernacle altar, but God accepted it because of the extraordinary circumstances.
The sacrifice at Beth-shemesh was no violation of the law, because the ark itself was the throne of God's presence and made the ground a valid altar.

notes.meaning: Because Beth-shemesh was a town designated for priests, Levites were on hand to care for the holy objects properly. They lifted the ark and the chest of gold down and set them safely on the rock, while the townspeople presented additional sacrifices of praise.

The five Philistine rulers watched everything from a distance until the ark was welcomed into Israel. With their questions answered and God's power made clear, they traveled back home to Ekron that very day.

The writer records that the Philistines returned five golden tumors, one for each of their five major cities. Each capital city had to give an offering, showing that every part of their nation had suffered under God's hand.

Golden rats were sent not only for the five walled cities but also for the surrounding country villages that were ravaged by the pests. The large stone where the ark rested remained in Joshua's field for many years as a lasting monument of how God brought His ark back home.

The celebration turned into tragedy when some of the men treated the sacred ark with careless curiosity and looked inside. The Lord struck down seventy men for this irreverence, reminding Israel that His holy presence must never be treated like an ordinary object.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The number 50,070 found in some manuscripts is widely seen as an early copyist's error, with seventy being the original number of men who died in the village.

notes.meaning: Shaken by the sudden deaths, the survivors cried out that no one could survive in the presence of such a holy God. Instead of humbly turning away from their sin, they reacted with dread and looked for a way to get rid of the ark.

The men of Beth-shemesh sent a message to the nearby hill town of Kiriath-jearim, pleading with them to come take the ark away. Because they were terrified of God's holiness, they treated His presence as a dangerous burden instead of a great blessing.
